'''Veronica Vaida''' (born August 3, 1950) is a Romanian-Hungarian-American chemist and professor at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]]. She is an expert in [[environmental chemistry]] and aerosols.

==Early life and education==
Vaida was born in [[Bucharest]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|author=Vaida, Veronica|date=2018-02-08|title=Veronica Vaida: Autobiographical Notes|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=122|issue=5|pages=1159–1166|doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.7b12802|pmid=29415545|issn=1089-5639|oclc=970486961|bibcode=2018JPCA..122.1159V}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sV03bFwxm7wC&pg=PA228|title=Will to Freedom: A Perilous Journey Through Fascism and Communism|author=Balas, Egon|date=2008|publisher=Syracuse University Press|isbn=9780815609308}}</ref> Her parents were Hungarians from [[Transylvania]] and met after [[World War II]].<ref name=":0"/> Her mother, Elza Katz, survived an [[Auschwitz concentration camp]] and her father [[Vasile Vaida]] was a political prisoner.<ref name=":0"/> She attended a Hungarian school in [[Cluj-Napoca|Cluj]] and moved back to Bucharest in 1963.<ref name=":0"/> She studied chemistry at the [[University of Bucharest]].<ref name=":0"/> After seeing a US position advertised in 1969, she moved to [[Brown University]], working on detectors for molecular beams.<ref name=":0"/> She joined [[Yale University]] for her postgraduate studies in 1973, but struggled to find an academic mentor because the male academics thought organic chemistry was "unsuitable for women".<ref name=":0"/> Her original mentor was [[Geraldine A. Kenney-Wallace]], who left to set up the first ultrafast spectroscopy lab at the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name=":0"/> She eventually obtained her Ph.D. from [[Yale University]] in 1977.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://chem.colorado.edu/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=288:veronica-vaida&catid=41:faculty&Itemid=93|title=Biography|publisher=[[University of Colorado]]|access-date=June 15, 2013|archive-date=March 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160319133800/http://chem.colorado.edu/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=288:veronica-vaida&catid=41:faculty&Itemid=93|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1977 Vaida became a [[Xerox]] postdoctoral fellow at [[Harvard University]], working alongside [[Dudley R. Herschbach]] and Bill Reinhart on photoreaction dynamics.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.euchems.eu/european-chemistry-gold-medal-meet-international-award-committee/|title=European Chemistry Gold Medal - Meet the International Award Committee - EuChemS|date=2017-07-06|work=EuChemS|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref> She collaborated with Kevin Peters and [[Meredith Applebury]] at [[Bell Labs]]. She was made a member of the faculty at [[Harvard University]] in 1978.<ref name=":0"/> In 1980 she was appointed an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] Fellow and a [[The Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation|Camille and Henry Dreyfus]] scholar in 1984.<ref name=":0"/><ref name=":1"/> Vaida developed jet cooled absorption spectrometry to analyse the lifetimes of reactive systems, where excited state dynamics were complicated because of diffuse absorption and limited fluorescence.<ref name=":0"/> She worked on an [[excimer laser]] that could allow her group to study transition metal complexes.<ref name=":0"/><ref name=":3">{{cite journal|author=Donaldson, D. James|author2=Francisco, Joseph S.|author3=Grassian, Vicki H.|author4=Hemley, Russell J.|author5=Jonas, David M.|author6=Leopold, Kenneth R.|author7=Levinger, Nancy E.|date=2018-02-08|title=Tribute to Veronica Vaida|journal=[[Journal of Physical Chemistry A]]|volume=122|issue=5|pages=1157–1158|doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.7b11829|pmid=29415548|bibcode=2018JPCA..122.1157D}}</ref> She moved to the [[University of Colorado Boulder]], where she built her own spectroscopy lab. She identified the excited state of OCIO with [[Susan Solomon]] in 1989.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Vaida, Veronica|author2=Solomon, Susan|author3=Richard, Erik C.|author4=Rühl, Eckart|author5=Jefferson, Anne|date=1989|title=Photoisomerization of OCIO: a possible mechanism for polar ozone depletion|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=342|issue=6248|pages=405–408|doi=10.1038/342405a0|issn=0028-0836|oclc=1076418075|bibcode=1989Natur.342..405V|s2cid=4262245}}</ref> After collaborating with [[Susan Solomon]], Vaida recognised that her studies of model compounds could be useful in atmospheric chemistry. Her group went on to study atmospheric ozone, water clusters and polar ice.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Vaida, Veronica|date=2011-07-14|title=Perspective: Water cluster mediated atmospheric chemistry|journal=[[The Journal of Chemical Physics]]|volume=135|issue=2|article-number=020901|doi=10.1063/1.3608919|pmid=21766916|issn=0021-9606|oclc=1057981142|bibcode=2011JChPh.135b0901V|doi-access=free}}</ref> She divorced Kevin Peters in 1990.<ref name=":0"/>

In 1994 she was awarded an [[Jack Erskine|Erskine fellowship]] at the [[University of Canterbury]] in [[New Zealand]].<ref name=":1"/> She worked on the overtones of OH vibrations using a [[Cavity ring-down spectroscopy|cavity ring down spectrometer]].<ref name=":0"/> She went on to study organic fragments on aerosol particles.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Ellison, G. Barney|author2=Tuck, Adrian F.|author3=Vaida, Veronica|year=1999|title=Atmospheric processing of organic aerosols|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres|volume=104|issue=D9|pages=11633–11641|doi=10.1029/1999jd900073|issn=0148-0227|oclc=847054952|bibcode=1999JGR...10411633E|doi-access=free}}</ref> She hypothesised that aerosol coagulation and division permitted organics to form a surfactant layer on top of the aerosol and recognised that this was similar to single cell bacteria.<ref name=":0"/>

Her group began to study organic films at aerosol water-air interfaces, using surface reflection infrared spectroscopy to examine differences in phenylalanine ionisation in the bulk and at the water surface.<ref name=":0"/> Vaida's Ph.D. student, [[Elizabeth Griffith (chemist)|Elizabeth Griffith]], found that peptide bonds at the surface of water would be generated nonenzymatically.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Donaldson, D. J.|author2=Vaida, Veronica|date=April 2006|title=The Influence of Organic Films at the Air−Aqueous Boundary on Atmospheric Processes|journal=[[Chemical Reviews]]|volume=106|issue=4|pages=1445–1461|doi=10.1021/cr040367c|pmid=16608186|issn=0009-2665|oclc=896847472}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Griffith, Elizabeth C.|author2=Shoemaker, Richard K.|author3=Vaida, Veronica|title=Sunlight-initiated Chemistry of Aqueous Pyruvic Acid: Building Complexity in the Origin of Life|journal=[[Origins of Life and Evolution of Biospheres]]|volume=43|issue=4–5|pages=341–352|doi=10.1007/s11084-013-9349-y|issn=0169-6149|oclc=183275831|pmid=24362712|year=2013|bibcode=2013OLEB...43..341G|s2cid=3124107}}</ref> In 2007 she was appointed distinguished lecturer at [[Sigma Xi]] Distinguished Lecturer [[University of Colorado Boulder]].<ref name=":1"/> She studied how sunlight can abiotically provide the prebiotic reactions essential for the evolution of life.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Vaida, Veronica|date=2016-08-12|title=Atmospheric radical chemistry revisited|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=353|issue=6300|pages=650|doi=10.1126/science.aah4111|issn=0036-8075|pmid=27516586|bibcode=2016Sci...353..650V|s2cid=206651763}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Rapf, Rebecca J.|author2=Vaida, Veronica|year=2016|title=Sunlight as an energetic driver in the synthesis of molecules necessary for life|journal=[[Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics]]|volume=18|issue=30|pages=20067–20084|doi=10.1039/C6CP00980H|pmid=27193698|issn=1463-9076|oclc=442203075|bibcode=2016PCCP...1820067R}}</ref> In 2018 the ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry A]]'' published a tribute to Vaida and her research.<ref name=":3"/>

===Awards and fellowships===
*2004 &ndash; Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.colorado.edu/lab/vaidagroup/veronica-vaida|title=Veronica Vaida|date=2016-01-11|work=Vaida Group|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref>
*2004 &ndash; Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref name=":2">{{cite journal|author=Vaida, Veronica|date=2018-02-08|title=Curriculum Vita of Veronica Vaida|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=122|issue=5|pages=1167|doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.7b12019|pmid=29415546|bibcode=2018JPCA..122.1167V|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*2004 &ndash; Fellow of the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://experts.colorado.edu/display/recip_413|title=(Vaida, Veronica - 2004) -- Radcliffe Institute Fellowship|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref>
*2004 &ndash; Fellow of the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/veronica-vaida/|title=Veronica Vaida|publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref>
*2011 &ndash; [[American Chemical Society]] [[E. Bright Wilson Award in Spectroscopy|E. Bright Wilson Award]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/e-bright-wilson-award-in-spectroscopy.html|title=E. Bright Wilson Award in Spectroscopy - American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref>
*2020 &ndash; [[American Chemical Society]] Irving Langmuir Award in Chemical Physics<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/irving-langmuir-award-in-chemical-physics.html|title=Irving Langmuir Award in Chemical Physics - American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=2020-04-28}}</ref>
*2020 &ndash; Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200428010617/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 28, 2020|title=2020 NAS Election|website=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=2020-04-28}}</ref>

==Personal life==
She married Kevin Peters, a colleague in the chemistry department at Harvard University in 1978. They divorced in 1990. In 1993 she met Adrian Tuck, a chemist at the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] Atmospheric Lab. They married in 1997.<ref name=":0"/>
